articles.title: ‘Wolf of Wall Street’ Jordan Belfort on his AI salespeople who are better than humans: ‘What if you have a bad apple that says stuff?’
articles.summary: Belfort told Fortune that his AI voice startup, Tone, has about $1 million in revenue, $10 million raised, and an API launching in about a week.
articles.body:
Just months after Jordan Belfort's court-ordered restitution obligation ended, leaving his victims far short of the $110 million he was ordered to pay them, "The Wolf of Wall Street" is selling over the phone again, this time with AI bots trained on his sales techniques.

Belfort's new AI sales-voice startup, Tone, has brought in about $1 million in revenue so far, and he's aiming for between $20 million and $30 million in recurring revenue within the next year.

Belfort said Tone's technology is more reliable than humans because companies can keep a firm grip on what it says. This contrasts with salespeople who can stray from approved scripts and could potentially cross a line with customers.

"What if you have a bad apple that says stuff—maybe inadvertently even, right?" he said.

Tone launched publicly on Nov. 16 with about $10 million raised, and Belfort said its API and a content creation platform goes live in about a week. It arrives as big companies move to automate customer calls— Verizon CEO Dan Schulman told Fortune this month the telecom giant is preparing to automate much of its routine customer service work—and two years after the FCC put AI-generated voices under federal robocall rules. A study by international cloud voice software company AVOXI found in September that just over half of organizations are already using AI voice agents, and a majority are planning to adopt them over the next two years.

Tone's offerings include 16 different male and female artificial voices ranging from higher to lower-pitched that are trained on Belfort's tonal sales techniques. Unlike other AI voices, he said they adjust their intonation and volume, among other factors, to try to better influence listeners.

This includes phrasing declarative statements as questions to show the listener you're engaged, or speaking in a low voice to convey scarcity and the importance of the information, Belfort told Fortune . Those subtle vocal techniques, he argued, can make the difference between someone listening to a sales pitch or hanging up and will help the company compete against an increasingly crowded field of voice AI startups. The tech is not meant to replace salespeople but merely to expand the number of contacts they can reach, he added.

Of the $10 million the company has raised ( TechCrunch first reported the figure), 70% of it came from friends and family and the rest from investors, he estimated.

Yet Belfort also noted that Tone still has limitations, especially when it comes to navigating complicated conversations.

articles.title: Quem são os 7 fundadores da Anthropic prestes a virar multibilionários | G1
articles.standfirst: A empresa de inteligência artificial por trás do Claude está prestes a vender suas ações na Bolsa dos EUA, tornando seus fundadores muito ricos.
articles.summary: A empresa de inteligência artificial por trás do Claude está prestes a vender suas ações na Bolsa dos EUA, tornando seus fundadores muito ricos.
articles.body:
Os irmãos Dario e Daniela Amodei fundaram juntos a empresa. — Foto: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images via BBC

Em apenas cinco anos, a Anthropic passou de uma startup desconhecida a uma gigante da tecnologia, avaliada em mais de US$ 1 trilhão.

A empresa por trás da plataforma de inteligência artificial (IA) Claude foi formada por sete pessoas que deixaram a concorrente OpenAI em 2021 e, em questão de horas, se tornarão multibilionárias — pelo menos no papel.

A Anthropic está abrindo o capital da empresa na bolsa de valores dos EUA e venderá suas ações por um preço entre US$ 70 e US$ 78 cada.

Pelo preço mais alto, as participações acionárias dos fundadores valerão pelo menos US$ 18,5 bilhões cada uma.

Então, quem são essas pessoas, todas na faixa dos trinta e quarenta anos, que estão prestes a ficar incrivelmente ricas?

Em 2020, Dario Amodei trabalhava na OpenAI , a empresa que popularizou a inteligência artificial generativa, quando lançou o Chat-GPT.

Ele decidiu que queria fazer as coisas do seu jeito e foi embora, levando consigo sua irmã Daniela e cinco colegas.

Amodei cresceu em São Francisco, impressionando os colegas de escola não apenas com seu talento acadêmico, mas também com sua velocidade na pista de corrida e sua preocupação com questões filosóficas e tecnológicas, incluindo o potencial das máquinas para adquirir consciência e a longevidade humana.

Inicialmente, ele estudou Física em Princeton e Stanford. Mas, após a morte de seu pai por hepatite C, ele mudou para Biologia e Ciências Biomédicas.

Antes de ingressar na OpenAI , Amodei trabalhou na gigante chinesa de tecnologia Baidu e no Google .

Mas ele disse que começou a se preocupar com o fato de algumas pessoas dentro da empresa estarem priorizando o lucro em detrimento da segurança , o que o levou a tomar a decisão de abandonar o barco.

Agora, com 43 anos, ele é o diretor executivo da Anthropic e a pessoa que, nas palavras de sua irmã, torna a empresa "ambiciosa".

Dario e Daniela Amodei eram muito próximos desde a infância e, mais tarde, dividiram um apartamento em São Francisco com outros amigos. Ela o acompanhou na OpenAI e se juntou a ele quando ele saiu para fundar a Anthropic.

Ela e o irmão sempre gostaram muito um do outro, diz ela, mas a única coisa que ela fez primeiro foi quando ela tornar vegetariana e ele fez isso também.

Amodei estudou Literatura Inglesa na Universidade da Califórnia em Santa Cruz, e, posteriormente, trabalhou para o ex-deputado democrata Matt Cartwright.

Ela também trabalhou na plataforma de serviços financeiros Stripe, onde foi chefe de operações de risco.

Aos 39 anos, ele é presidente da Anthropic, gerencia a equipe executiva e lidera as áreas de pesquisa, engenharia, produto, governança e comercial da empresa.

Tom Brown, um dos fundadores da Anthropic. — Foto: Cornell Watson/Bloomberg/Getty Images via BBC

Tom Brown, agora com 39 anos, seguiu os irmãos Amodei quando eles saíram para fundar seu novo negócio.

Ele liderou a engenharia do GPT-3 na OpenAI e, antes disso, trabalhou no projeto DeepMind do Google .

Brown consolidou suas credenciais empreendedoras ao cofundar um aplicativo chamado Grouper, que ajuda a organizar encontros para tomar bebidas entre grupos de amigos.

Ele apoiou a defesa do presidente Donald Trump sobre os datacenters, argumentando que eles são "uma enorme fonte de prosperidade".

Agora, como diretor de computação da Anthropic, ele é responsável pela forma como a empresa protege e utiliza seus recursos computacionais.

Jack Clark, um dos fundadores da Anthropic. — Foto: Peerapon Boonyakiat/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images via BBC

Jack Clark é outro graduado em artes entre os membros fundadores da startup original e o único que não é da América do Norte.

Natural de Brighton, no Reino Unido, estudou literatura inglesa e escrita criativa na Universidade de East Anglia e tornou-se jornalista de tecnologia, escrevendo para publicações como ZDNet UK, The Register e Bloomberg.

Ele se deixou contagiar pelo entusiasmo da inteligência artificial e ingressou na OpenAI , onde trabalhou inicialmente na área de comunicação, tornando-se posteriormente diretor de políticas.

Agora, com 37 anos, Clark é chefe da área de relações públicas na Anthropic. Ele também lidera o Instituto Anthropic, um centro de estudos sobre inteligência artificial.

Jared Kaplan, diretor científico da Anthropic. — Foto: Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg/Getty Images via BBC

Jared Kaplan, de 42 anos, é diretor científico da Anthropic e chefia sua pesquisa técnica. Ele também é professor associado na Universidade Johns Hopkins, em Baltimore.

Ele tem doutorado em física pela Universidade Harvard, nos Estados Unidos.

De acordo com a Anthropic, seu trabalho sobre leis de escala — que descrevem padrões matemáticos que mostram que modelos de IA maiores, treinados com mais dados, tendem a ser mais consistentes — ajudou a fornecer às empresas do setor uma estrutura para prever o comportamento da tecnologia.

Chris Olah, líder de pesquisa em interpretabilidade da Anthropic. — Foto: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty Images via BBC

Chris Olah é descrito como "líder de pesquisa em interpretabilidade", com foco principal em como os modelos de IA interagem entre si.

Mas, de acordo com o New York Times, Olah passou grande parte do último ano convocando reuniões com líderes religiosos.

Descrito pelo jornal como "com aparência juvenil", mas com "o zelo de um evangelista", o jovem de 34 anos estaria explorando a relação entre moralidade e inteligência artificial.

Ele liderou anteriormente a pesquisa de interoperabilidade na OpenAI e, antes disso, foi cientista pesquisador no Google Brain.

O canadense abandonou a Universidade de Toronto antes do previsto, mas posteriormente garantiu uma bolsa Thiel de US$ 100 mil, destinada a ajudar pessoas talentosas a ingressarem na pesquisa sem a necessidade de um diploma.

Sam McCandlish, um dos fundadores da Anthropic. — Foto: Divulgação/Anthropic via BBC

Sam McCandlish, de 36 anos, tem um papel menos público do que os outros fundadores, mas, assim como eles, deterá cerca de 1,6% da empresa após a abertura de capital.

Como resultado, ele também verá sua participação se consolidar em um ativo extremamente valioso.

McCandlish é o arquiteto-chefe da Anthropic e ajuda a moldar e implementar a política da empresa destinada a mitigar os riscos da IA. Anteriormente, trabalhou na área de segurança da OpenAI .

Ele tem doutorado em física pela Universidade de Stanford e é graduado em matemática e física pela Universidade de Brandeis, nos arredores de Boston.

articles.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol artificial intelligence models
articles.summary: OpenAI has launched two new artificial intelligence models, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, designed for different types of users and tasks.
articles.body: OpenAI has launched two new artificial intelligence models, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, designed for different types of users and tasks. While Astra is built for complex professional work, scientific research, coding and advanced projects, Sol is aimed at everyday tasks and faster workflows. The company said both models deliver better results on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens, helping users complete more work within their usage limits. OpenAI also highlighted lower costs for businesses and developers using the models at scale.OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra focuses on complex professional workOpenAI describes GPT-6.2 Astra as its most capable model yet for complex professional tasks. It is designed to create better presentations, spreadsheets and documents that follow industry standards and user-provided templates. The model also brings improvements in coding, website development, gaming and 3D design. According to OpenAI, its writing is more direct, with fewer generic conclusions and unnecessary details.On the Agents' Last Exam benchmark, which evaluates models on complex, multi-step professional tasks, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher than its predecessor, GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI said it achieved this result at less than one-third of the cost.The company also reported improvements in scientific research capabilities. GPT-6.2 Astra achieved a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science, a test that measures how well AI models carry out scientific research tasks using computer terminals.‘OpenAI GPT-6.2 Sol designed for everyday tasks’The second model, GPT-6.2 Sol, is designed for everyday work and general-purpose use. It improves on GPT-6.1 Sol in reasoning, efficiency and handling multi-step tasks. OpenAI said the model can help with both technical and non-technical work, including writing, coding and research.On the LifeVal benchmark, which tests AI performance on practical everyday tasks such as finding suitable schools, comparing homes and planning meals, GPT-6.2 Sol scored higher than GPT-6 Astra while costing about one-seventh as much.GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol AI models: Pricing and availabilityGPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are available to Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users through ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access both models through the OpenAI API.OpenAI has priced GPT-6.2 Astra's API usage 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra. Its rates are $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Cached input costs $0.40 per million tokens. GPT-6.2 Sol retains the API pricing of its predecessor, GPT-6.1 Sol, at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.OpenAI also said both models have stronger cybersecurity capabilities and meet its High threshold for biological and chemical capabilities under its Preparedness Framework. The company has introduced additional safeguards to reduce the risk of misuse.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Who is Han Won-seok? Meet South Korea's top tax accountant exam scorer who admitted to cheating with hidden camera and AI
articles.summary: A near-perfect score, a coveted professional qualification, and a remarkable academic achievement — and despite that significant feat, all of it has
articles.body: A near-perfect score, a coveted professional qualification, and a remarkable academic achievement — and despite that significant feat, all of it has turned into a national cheating scandal in South Korea!Han Won-seok, a 34-year-old candidate who topped the country's national certified tax accountant examination, has admitted to using a miniature hidden camera, a smartphone, and generative artificial intelligence (AI) to cheat in both stages of the examination, as reported by the BBC.What happened?Han Won-seok’s story has flipped South Korea’s exam system on its head. Why so? He wasn’t just another ambitious candidate trying his luck. No, he was the guy who blew past almost every question in the national tax accountant exam, missing just one in the first round and coming out on top in the finals.In case one wants the numbers, in the first stage of the certified tax accountant examination, held in April 2026, Han answered 159 out of 160 questions correctly, securing 397.5 out of 400 marks. He followed this up with 663 out of 800 in the second-stage written examination in July, eventually emerging as the overall topper.People applauded his near-perfect scores at first, but then suspicion started buzzing online. The numbers looked almost impossible, even for the smartest people in the profession. But then came the truth.Who is Han Won-seok?According to The Korea Times, Han, a 34-year-old trying to reinvent himself after leaving a steady corporate job, put himself in the spotlight. In multiple interviews, Han said that he’d aced everything on his own, relying on self-study, but some veteran accountants began to poke holes in his story. They wondered: How could someone pull this off without any help, especially considering the exam’s brutal difficulty?But after brushing off the rumors for a while, Han finally came clean.How did Han use a hidden camera and AI to cheat in the exam?In a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, he admitted he’d used a hidden miniature camera, a smartphone, and an AI tool to cheat. Basically, he snapped photos of exam questions, sent them off to the AI, and checked the answers on his phone. It wasn’t just a one-time stunt; the same method had gotten him through both rounds of the tax accountant exam, and he’d tried it earlier in the public accountant exam, too. Some thought he’d used smart glasses, but he clarified it was actually a camera and phone. Han kept the nuts and bolts of his setup secret, worried that someone else might copy his method.The aftermath of the confessionAs soon as Han’s confession dropped, the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency kicked off a formal investigation. He turned in a written confession and promised to cooperate, even showing up for questioning a couple of days later. The Human Resources Development Service, which runs the exam, found itself in the crosshairs. None of the four invigilators assigned to Han reported anything suspicious, and the agency had to publicly apologize for missing the cheating. They’re now filing a criminal complaint against him, accusing him of obstructing their work.Why did Han do it?Han disclosed his motivations in the video itself. After leaving his corporate gig to start a business, things went downhill fast with rising costs, fallout from global events like the Russia-Ukraine war, and more. As money got tight, he felt ashamed for disappointing his parents, and the uncertainty about how long it would take to get the qualification made it worse. Han admitted he was desperate to make his family proud and needed a way out. The pressure got the best of him, and cheating felt like the shortcut. He apologized, acknowledging the unfair advantage he had over others who studied honestly.What action is South Korea taking?Now, this scandal couldn’t have landed at a more sensitive time. South Korea is days away from holding its massive college entrance exam, Suneung. More than half a million students are gearing up for it, and in this country, results shape futures: who gets into the right school, who lands the best jobs, even social status, etc.Now that the scandal has shaken the country, the government is scrambling to tighten security. Invigilators will check glasses and button stickers for hidden cameras, inspect collars, and use metal detectors for anything suspicious. Bags and personal belongings stay outside. Surveillance is getting bumped up, with nearly 8,400 more exam monitors on duty. During the exam, every phone in the country will receive an emergency alert aimed at rooting out any hidden electronics. AI companies handling chatbots are cooperating, promising to help track if anyone uploads exam questions.And if someone gets caught cheating in the university entrance exam now, they’ll be banned for ten years.What’s next for Han Won-seok?South Korean law says candidates found cheating lose their results and can’t retake the exam for five years. As of now, the Ministry of Finance and Economy is moving quickly to revoke his certificate. Criminal charges may follow, depending on how the investigation unfolds.But beyond that, in the age of AI, this scandal exposes a huge gap between the old ways of supervising exams and the new tricks people can pull with AI and tiny devices. The debate isn’t just about fairness anymore. It’s about whether we can trust exam results in a world where technology keeps slipping past security.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Suno now lets you make AI videos for your AI music
articles.summary: Suno has introduced image and video generation in its latest effort to expand beyond being an AI music platform.
articles.body: Suno has introduced image and video generation in its latest effort to expand beyond being an AI music platform. The new feature, called “Visuals,” allows users to turn Suno songs into AI-generated video clips that automatically lipsync to lyrics, or make images via prompt descriptions that can be used as thumbnails and album artwork. Visuals is available on web, iOS, and Android. The exact layout differs across Suno’s desktop and mobile interfaces, but users will find a new Visuals tab under Create mode on each version. Web users can also access Visuals by selecting the three dot menu on a song in their library. From there, users can select which section of the track to use, up to a maximum of 15 seconds, and select a reference image to build the generated video clip. There are three options available for the starting image reference: selecting one of the original character presets provided by Suno, uploading your own photo or artwork, or generating the image directly on Suno using descriptive prompts. The image generation capabilities also allow users to select specific aspect ratios, optimizing results for landscape or portrait modes and online platforms. [Media: For video generation, users can select whether the reference image is used as the start or end frame, making it easier to edit the 15-second clips together. There’s a toggle to automatically lipsync vocals to the generated video, and tools for adjusting aspect ratio and clip length. Visuals also includes a dedicated video editing timeline for assembling clips into longer videos, and adding customizable song lyric text. The H3 Move AI model is being used to power Visuals, based on H3 from MiniMax. Suno says the AI has been “optimized for our community including adding additional protections and safeguards,” which include a “suite of new text and visual filters” designed to block people from using or generating the likeness of specific artists, public figures, copyrighted works and IP. Visuals also uses its own “Visuals credits” to generate videos and images, which are distinct from the song credits used to make AI music, meaning Suno users will have additional expenses to pay in order to use this new feature. The Visuals launch follows Suno introducing a Speech feature in October for generating spoken words and voiceovers. Adding video capabilities is another attempt to diversify the platform after Suno’s music generator attracted a number of high-profile lawsuits, though it seems some users would rather the company focus on improving those song-generating capabilities. In the YouTube video for the Visuals launch, one user says “FIX AUDIO BEFORE ADDING CRAP NOBODY ASKED FOR” — a sentiment that other commenters are echoing.

articles.title: Nvidia clarifies when it will — and won't — keep financing neoclouds | TechCrunch
articles.summary: If Nvidia is backstopping a data center loan, it won't be on the hook unless the neocould has independent financing and gets the facility built, with Nvidia gear installed, interim CEO Colette Kress explained.
articles.body:
One reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it.

And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter , which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter.

But Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the company aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance new data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, announced in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company said.

Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking . She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion.

Under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the company is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she said.

“There is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and or debt, in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” Kress said to analysts on Tuesday during the quarterly conference call.

She pointed to OpenAI PORTS-Pike campus as an example of where such terms apply. When asked, she also said this wasn’t a change in policy, but simply a clarification of existing terms. However, these disclosures have never been public before.

Kress also made clear that Nvidia wasn’t bailing on all the ways it was financing the AI boom, especially new data centers. But, she said, Nvidia was going to be far more selective in the future.

“The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That’s a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities,” she said. At the same time, she insisted that Nvidia was “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing.”

One of the ongoing criticisms Huang faced was his love of circular deals: invest in his customers so they would turn around and buy his products . Kress is now trying to strike a delicate balance. She isn’t saying she will pull the rug out from under Nvidia’s customers. After all, the company’s investments undoubtedly spurred the AI boom that has been so lucrative for Nvidia. But she’s also signaling that the days of Huang’s freewheeling dealmaking may be over .

articles.title: Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
articles.summary: Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year.
articles.body: Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China. “Our guidance ⁠does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping ​licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future. The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 ⁠H200 chips ​were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology.

articles.title: Hacks, AI or overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
articles.summary: There is no evidence these are linked, but the constant series of tech disruptions can be unnerving.
articles.body:
Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale.

These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked.

There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie.

As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.

A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.

It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.

Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.

Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.

But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.

AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.

And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.

Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.

Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.

"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.

In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.

This happened in the recent Java incident , as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.

These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.

Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.

A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.

With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.

Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.

In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.

"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."

In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.

At the same time, Anthropic, among other leading AI firms, has warned of the risks its own products pose .

Outages in particular have an impact on the physical world as they often cause disruption to healthcare, schools and people's ability to do their jobs.

Or, in the case over the weekend, planes' ability to fly.

They also shine a light on the world's heavy reliance on a small number of players.

Not just frontier AI companies, but infrastructure providers such as Microsoft and Amazon, which - along with Google - run a huge chunk of the world's computer servers.

In the PHP incident, the world was holding its breath as one programmer - working voluntarily - worked to issue patches in a form that was easily applicable.

And Java, run by another tech giant Oracle, is used by nearly all of the biggest companies on Earth.

"The Oracle Java vulnerability is a stark reminder of how dependent businesses have become on a relatively small number of critical technologies," said Sheila Pancholi, risk assurance lead at consultancy firm RSM UK.

"Organisations need to know where their critical technology dependencies sit, act quickly when vulnerabilities emerge, and test that their response has actually worked."

Meanwhile Xander Van Raemdonck, security engineer at Aikido Security, said the challenge was "knowing whether you're exposed".

"Java is bundled inside a huge amount of business software, so many companies don't have a full list of where it runs," he said.

The AI tools used to help find security flaws are still so new that they will probably continue to find vulnerabilities which have been lingering in code for decades.

"AI is accelerating discovery on both sides and speeding up how much software gets shipped," said Martin Reynolds, field CTO at software delivery company Harness.

"So the volume of what developers need to patch is going up, while the time they have to get the work done it is going down."

Tech debt will need to continue to be dealt with - which means more upgrades to systems and more potential for these to cause disruptions.

Plus there is the constant threat from hackers as they continue to get more sophisticated.

Attackers only need to find one vulnerability to exploit - whereas defenders have to protect against all potential hacks.

"Attackers can move quickly and carefree, and experiment without risk of failure so they can naturally often move a fraction faster," Helme said.

"We're currently observing that small delay between how fast the attackers can move and how fast the defenders can move."

The cat-and-mouse nature of the cyber-security game means it's unlikely to end any time soon - and the impact of AI means the stakes are getting higher.

articles.title: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires
articles.summary: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.
articles.body:
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.

If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.

Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.

But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.

Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.

He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.

The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

articles.title: Hollywood icon and ‘That ’70s Show’ star could become a billionaire from Anthropic IPO; his firm’s $435M bet is now worth $7B
articles.summary: The actor’s early bet on artificial intelligence could put him in rare company alongside Tyler Perry, Jerry Seinfeld and Arnold Schwarzenegger.
articles.body:
Ashton Kutcher could be on his way to billionaire status.

The 48-year-old actor stands to be one of the biggest winners as Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude assistant, prepares to go public at a proposed $1.4 trillion valuation, according to Page Six . Sound Ventures, the venture capital firm Kutcher co-founded, has invested about $435 million in Anthropic, and that stake is now reportedly worth about $7 billion, per Newsweek .

Sound Ventures first backed Anthropic in 2023, after Kutcher and his business partner Guy Oseary met with the company's CEO, Dario Amodei, Bloomberg reported. The firm kept investing in later rounds and now owns roughly 0.5% of the company.

Kutcher won't walk away with a $7 billion check, though. Sound Ventures manages money for outside investors, so any profits will be split among several parties.

Ashton Kutcher's History as a Tech Investor

Kutcher has quietly become one of Hollywood's most successful tech investors, with a reported net worth of more than $200 million. In 2010, he co-founded A-Grade Investments with billionaire Ron Burkle and Oseary, the longtime manager of Madonna and the Red Hot Chili Peppers. Their early bets included Spotify, Uber and Airbnb, and they reportedly grew $30 million into about $250 million, per Newsweek .

Kutcher and Oseary launched Sound Ventures in 2015 as A-Grade's successor. In July, Kutcher stepped down as a partner but stayed on as a senior advisor. The Wall Street Journal reported the decision was partly over differing views on which startups to back: the firm wanted more established companies, while Kutcher prefers early-stage ones. He has since launched a new fund with Morgan Beller, a former co-leader of Meta's Libra project.

Musicians such as Taylor Swift, Beyoncé and Dr. Dre have reached billionaire status, but it's far rarer for actors. According to Forbes , the film industry's billionaires include Tyler Perry, Jerry Seinfeld and Arnold Schwarzenegger.

Kutcher has been married to his former That '70s Show co-star Mila Kunis since 2015. The couple share two children, daughter Wyatt and son Dimitri.

articles.title: Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
articles.summary: Nvidia and AMD earnings show booming demand. This is why a frontier slowdown might not derail it.
articles.body: This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the most powerful AI models, warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become harder for their own creators to control. It was a strange moment for the AI boom. The people building the most powerful models were warning about what those models might be capable of, and investors were suddenly wondering what would happen to chip demand if the labs eased up on new models. US chip stocks bore the brunt of the sell-off. Despite the hubbub it created, whatever slowdown there was appears to have been short-lived. OpenAI had announced only a two-week pause; it restarted the run 10 days later, at the end of August, though it continued to “temporarily hold back some smaller experimental training runs.” Anthropic released upgraded versions of its Fable and Mythos frontier models in November, touting improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. And the companies selling the chips powering those advances are doing better than ever. Nvidia on Tuesday posted a blockbuster quarter, with data center revenue rising 110 percent from a year ago to $107.6 billion in the three months ended October 25. The chip designer began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” The Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments alone. The racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle. Meta plans to expand Vera Rubin deployments to train and run AI models and agents. Nvidia name-dropped Anthropic and OpenAI, too. Anthropic has expanded access to Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers and continues to work with Nvidia on future chip designs tailored to its workloads. OpenAI is among the companies adopting Nvidia’s new Vera CPUs. “Proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic continue to advance the frontier,” Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on the earnings call. She said the company expects major frontier labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its data center revenue this fiscal year. Nvidia also raised its revenue growth forecast for next fiscal year from 70 percent to 75 percent. Chipmaker AMD, meanwhile, reported its biggest quarter ever earlier this month, with revenue up 45 percent to $13.4 billion. Data center sales drove that growth, nearly doubling to $8.5 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic were among the first customers running workloads on AMD’s new high-end Helios systems, which use its latest MI450 GPUs. Broadcom, which helps many of the biggest AI companies design their own custom chips, has yet to report earnings. But so far, there’s little sign of a frontier slowdown hurting chip sales. Of course, even if AI labs were to significantly scale back their training ambitions, it would take a while to show up in chipmakers’ earnings. Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told The Verge in September that it would take about six months to see the financial effects of a slowdown, owing to existing computing and memory procurement agreements. The impact could show up sooner in orders placed with chip manufacturers like TSMC. So far, there’s little evidence of that, either: TSMC’s latest sales figures also show continued strength. But there’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have. “While one might argue the need for top-end GPUs will reduce with this shift toward inferencing, these workloads will collectively require more compute infrastructure than training,” Shah said. “Overall, it means a net increase in demand for all types of accelerators.” According to our analysis of the latest data from corporate spending platform Ramp, frontier model families accounted for about 60 percent of token usage among businesses using Ramp in early November — a record high and about three times their share at the start of the year. That includes OpenAI’s Astra and Sol models and Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models. But even as businesses use more AI, their spending is only growing modestly. “It’s not really a demand issue though,” Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, tells The Verge. “By all measures, companies are using more AI.” Rather, competition among AI model providers is driving down token prices so rapidly that it’s calling OpenAI and Anthropic’s revenue projections into question, Kharazian says. That could prove beneficial for the companies supplying computing power. On Nvidia’s earnings call, Kress said token prices had fallen nearly 60 percent since May, spurring more usage. Meanwhile, rental prices for Nvidia GPUs across generations have gone up. Nvidia and AMD are positioning their most powerful chips for both training and inference, including the demanding workloads created by AI agents. That doesn’t necessarily mean Nvidia will maintain its dominance. As AI companies get more serious about the economics of serving their models to millions of people, they’re increasingly turning to custom chips that can do so more cheaply than general-purpose GPUs. Counterpoint expects shipments of custom AI server processors to surpass those of data center GPUs by 2028. “Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend,” Shah said. Indeed, on Nvidia’s earnings call, UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked Kress whether the company would be willing to sacrifice some of its hefty profit margins as frontier labs increasingly invest in custom chips and prioritize computing efficiency. Kress maintained that Nvidia’s systems justify their pricing and reiterated the company’s gross margin outlook. For companies like Nvidia, the bigger threat may not be that AI companies slow down, but that they find cheaper chips on which to keep going.

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it's 'hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals, including an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
articles.body:
The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns.

Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel.

“Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”

OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology.

Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.”

“I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.”

Huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people , including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that they do not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.

Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.”

“I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman said. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s Wall Street debut marks a new chapter for AI
articles.summary: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, is expected to go public Thursday in what could be the largest stock market debut of all time.
articles.body: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, is expected to go public Thursday in what could be the largest stock market debut of all time. The blockbuster IPO underscores the enormous amount of money being invested in AI, and the growing influence that the technology has on everything from the stock market to the broader US economy. The AI developer is targeting a range of $70 to $78 a share for the 825 million shares it plans to sell in its IPO. At the upper range, Anthropic would bring in as much as $64.4 billion and fetch a market valuation of up to $1.4 trillion — enormous figures for a company founded just under six years ago, reflecting the excitement around AI. The company is expected to confirm the final pricing later Wednesday. The offering comes alongside a separate $26 billion investment from major tech companies like Nvidia, bringing the total amount raised to $90.4 billion — a figure that would surpass SpaceX’s record-setting $75 billion IPO earlier this year. That’s before additional options for banks to sell more shares, which could lift Anthropic’s total haul to $100 billion — more than SpaceX’s total $86 billion figure. The third- and fourth-largest IPOs of all time are Saudi Aramco at $29.4 billion in 2019 and SK Hynix at $26.5 billion this year. “SpaceX was the largest IPO in history by a wide margin, and Anthropic might be exceeding SpaceX. Both of them are much bigger than any previous IPO,” said Jay Ritter, professor emeritus and director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida. “What’s also remarkable is that Anthropic is less than six years old.” The $1.4 trillion target valuation would catapult Anthropic into the ranks of the world’s 12 largest publicly traded companies. It will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT.” From startup to trillion-dollar company Anthropic was founded in 2021 when a group of employees at OpenAI left to start a new company with a focus on AI safety. That startup released its first version of Claude to the public in March 2023, a few months after OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public in November 2022. When Anthropic released Claude Code in early 2025, it quickly gained traction with software developers. Revenue continued to soar after the launch of Claude Cowork in early 2026 and as Anthropic established itself as a core provider of agentic AI tools. But, as a private company, there was less visibility into Anthropic’s finances. Going public means the company will now be required to disclose more information about its revenue, spending and losses every quarter, offering a pulse check on the health of the AI boom. The path to its public debut has not been without controversy. The Trump administration at one point barred Anthropic from releasing its advanced models to the public. Meanwhile, there are growing concerns about the potential for AI agents to go rogue and for the increasingly powerful technology to be used in harmful ways. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei spearheaded calls to “pace the frontier” of AI in September after former Anthropic employees sounded the alarm over concerns about safety at the AI lab. Anthropic as an AI bellwether Stock market strategists point to mid-October 2022 as the start of the AI bull market, which took off after ChatGPT was released on November 30, 2022. The Nasdaq Composite has gained roughly 135% since the start of the bull market, adding $26 trillion in market value. Now, one of the core AI companies is set to join the public markets. By going public, Anthropic is in part carrying the weight of the AI boom on its shoulders. Investors are keen to see how the frontier labs can turn their models into steady profit streams, justify enormous spending on the data center buildout and deliver returns. Anthropic earns revenue through companies and people using its Claude products. Anthropic’s revenue has experienced dramatic growth, helping the company fetch its more than $1 trillion-expected valuation and putting it are the forefront of how AI companies are trying to become profitable businesses. Anthropic is not profitable yet because it is still investing in its AI tools. Anthropic has spending commitments of roughly $900 billion in the coming years as it spends money to get compute power to train its cutting-edge AI models and support people using them. The company needs to lock in extraordinary revenue growth to justify its business model and valuation. Optimistic investors believe that demand for AI tools will continue to surge as more companies adopt the technology. Analysts expect Anthropic to pursue other methods for revenue growth, including the development of specialized models that can be used in industries such as health and science. But skeptics question whether the company can maintain its growth and revenue as competition intensifies. A bearish case for Anthropic is that AI tools are going to become more like a commodity, where customers can pick and choose between different providers with ease, making it difficult to retain strong pricing power and eating into revenue. The IPO also comes as enthusiasm for AI stocks is cooling: The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite is down more than 10% from its record high six weeks ago. Anthropic’s IPO could help restore confidence in the AI trade, which has been shaken in recent weeks by concerns about a slowdown to the data center buildout. But if it falls short of expectations, that could add to investors’ doubts. “Investor sentiment toward AI has been extremely volatile, and while a successful IPO will likely turn that sentiment positive in the near term, the long-term trajectory of Anthropic’s business and performance is what could really instill greater confidence in the AI trade,” said Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, a provider of pre-IPO research and IPO-focused ETFs.

articles.title: Sam Altman warns against a future where AI, not humans, calls the shots | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Sam Altman and Greg Brockman pushed back against Silicon Valley's growing debate over an AI takeover, while acknowledging the challenges of keeping advanced models under human control.
articles.body:
OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about whether there will be a gradual handover to AI — meaning AI will eventually become the decision-making authority across every major industry and institution.

“One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And I — we both — agree that that’s a terrible idea,” said Altman, who was sharing the stage with OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman.

The hand-off theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI. As existing AI technology builds newer, smarter generations, those will eventually become a superintelligence that humans can no longer control, the belief goes.

Altman explained that he and Brockman only disagree over how to best accomplish the goal of keeping humans in control, or what sort of challenges we should expect to face along the way. However, Altman characterized this as more of a debate between two people who share the same larger views.

“The question of how to actually prevent [handover] from happening — how to actually ensure that we will, given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do — that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way, and we don’t have this either accidental or intentional handover — I think we can both agree on that,” Altman said.

Brockman added that, as the models improve, there’s an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, and security, which may require changes in how things are currently done.

“Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new … technology,” he said.

Today, AI researchers monitor the model’s chain of thought, where the AI writes out what it’s thinking as it works through problems and performs tasks. But in Brockman’s view, that may not always be the best way to monitor more advanced AI that’s being built now.

“As the models have gotten more capable, they can do more within just the forward path without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring,” Brockman said. “We’re going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about, as the capabilities get to a certain point, chain-of-thought monitorability is degraded,” he continued, adding that all the problems were technical ones to be solved.

OpenAI had committed to increased chain-of-thought monitoring after the incident where an OpenAI model escaped containment and hacked into the AI model repository Hugging Face . In Wednesday’s interview, Brockman noted that the company told 25% of its production engineers to stop building things and work on securing the AI technology after the hack.

But despite the high-profile breach, he argued that forward progress was still critical to fight bad actors.

“I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities of models in the world, and you see cyber models that are coming from that are now … in the hands of threat actors everywhere, that I think that it’s really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend,” he said.

articles.title: AI data centers could consume more water than Americans drink in a year by 2030, says CEO working on solution
articles.summary: Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck says AI data centers could drink as much water as Americans by 2030 unless direct chip cooling and water recycling catch on.
articles.body: Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck, whose company is working on sustainable solutions to ecological problems like AI data centers’ robust water consumption, said that without reform, AI data centers could wind up consuming more water than Americans drink every year. "Ninety-five percent of the data centers today use a lot of water," he told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "We estimate that by 2030, with the old technologies in the U.S., we will use as much water to cool data centers as Americans are using for drinking needs." DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS Beck argued that this phenomenon is "not sustainable," and laid out the technologies his company is working on in an effort to reduce data centers’ water consumption. "Behind AI there's water in every step of the process. You need water to produce the chips, to power the chips and to cool the chips. And for the last four or five years, the chips generation that we were using were just cooled with air," he told Fox News Digital. However, with the increasing complexity of chips to match an ever-building demand for computer power, air conditioning alone is no longer sufficient to cool chips in data centers, Beck explained. "You need something that's way stronger. Water is 30 times better at extracting heat than air from the chips. So that's why many of those new data centers are moving toward direct chip water cooling, which ultimately is bringing cold water on top of the chip," he said. Direct water cooling, he explained, has the dual benefits of increasing efficiency and sustainability, because the water used to cool the chips can be recycled and used on every chip in a given data center. "So you end up in a place where you have a data center that is much more powerful [than] using no water, using less power, and ultimately not having an impact on natural resources and in communities around us, which is one of the unlocks that people are pushing back so much against right now," he said. ONE INDUSTRY FACES MULTI-TRILLION-DOLLAR RECKONING AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION RESHUFFLE On Nov. 4, voters across the U.S. elected lawmakers and executives who ran on campaigns to limit the number of data centers. In Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa upset incumbent Republican Greg Abbott. Voters who ticked the box for Hinojosa did so after she campaigned heavily on instituting a data center moratorium, a fact that Beck took note of. THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO "Most of the data centers that were installed in Texas or anywhere else in the country or in the world, for that matter, were using a lot of water, a lot of power. And that's created a lot of backlash from the communities, which is rightfully so," Beck told Fox News Digital. Beck noted that while Texas is one of the most economically strong states in the union, it is also one of the most water-stressed. "It's a bad combination," he said. "Obviously, high growth, great news; no water, less good news. So we've looked at those technological solutions on how do you bring higher growth, more data processing while using much less water." Beck added that the technologies Ecolab is developing will exclusively be used in new-build data centers, while the political pushback is surrounding the existing, more resource-demanding projects. Direct cooling allows for what is known as a closed loop system, a method that is far more sustainable and requires less water than previous iterations of water-cooling methods. Ecolab, Beck explained, has found a way to recycle water not only in the chip cooling process, but in chip fabrication as well, a process that necessitates extremely pure water. "The so-called fabs, they use huge amounts of water, which is very specialized water because it needs to be ultra pure," Beck explained. "And that, to be recycled, is even way harder than in a data center. But even there, at Ecolab we found solutions to not only get the highest purity of water to get the most advanced chips, but we can reuse that water as well in ways that are water neutral," he said. Beck also put in context just how pure the water for chip fabrication needs to be. "The purity is a million times more pure than what you would inject in your blood if it's a drug. So super high quality, super high purity of water at the end," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So the way we do it, in short, is ultimately at every step of the process we try to extract the water from that process step. We treat, we purify that water, we bring it back to an ultra-pure water level, and we bring back to the process. And the very special thing that we have at Ecolab, within that water you have some trace materials that we call connected water," he said. "So we understand the quality of the water throughout the process within the fab or the data center, for that matter, that we know exactly the quality of that water to make sure that the chips are perfectly produced. And we know what we need to do in order to re-treat that water so that it can be reused afterwards. And you end up with better chips, lower cost, and most importantly, water neutral," Beck said.
